t: Spreadsheets 1: structure, formatting, formulae and cell referencing
l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCSE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson L11: Spreadsheets 1: structure, formatting, formulae and cell referencing.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Identify cells, rows, columns, ranges and worksheets, and give a cell reference correctly. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

A spreadsheet is application software that stores data in a grid so that it can be calculated, analysed and presented. One spreadsheet file, called a workbook, can contain several worksheets, each shown on its own tab. A worksheet is made of columns, labelled with letters, and rows, labelled with numbers. The box where a column and a row cross is a cell.
Makes sense. Keep going.

Each cell has a cell reference, written column first and row second, so H8 means column H, row 8, just like co-ordinates in maths. A group of cells next to each other is a range, written with a colon between the first and last cell, for example B2 to B10. Cells can hold labels (text that explains what data means), values (numbers used in calculations), dates, formulae, or a reference to another cell. The big advantage of a spreadsheet over a paper table is automatic recalculation: when one value changes, every formula that depends on it is worked out again straight away.
Right. What else do we need to know?

Formatting changes how data looks without changing the value stored. A number can be shown as General, Number with a fixed number of decimal places, Currency (£), Percentage, Date or Time. Choosing the right format makes data easier to read and helps avoid mistakes: a cost column should be Currency, a discount Percentage, and a phone number Text so that the leading zero is kept. Percentage format shows 0.2 as 20 percent, so a rate typed as 20 percent is really stored as 0.2.
Got it. Keep going.

Presentation features include bold or larger fonts for headings, borders, fill colour, alignment, merge and centre for a title that runs across several columns, and wrap text so long labels fit inside a cell. Column widths can be changed so that nothing shows as ####. For printing, headers and footers can add a title, file name, date or page number to every page, and a print area can be set so that only the part of the sheet that matters is printed.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

A formula tells the spreadsheet what calculation to do. It must always begin with an equals sign, then use cell references, numbers and operators: plus to add, - to subtract, times to multiply, or to divide and ^ for a power. Brackets are calculated first, so =(B2+C2)/2 finds the mean of two cells. Using cell references rather than typing the numbers means that the answer updates when the data changes.
Okay. Keep going.

A function is a ready-made formula that does a particular job. SUM adds a range, AVERAGE finds the mean, MAX returns the largest value and MIN the smallest. COUNT counts how many cells in a range contain numbers, and COUNTIF counts only the cells that meet a condition, such as the formula on screen In each case the range goes inside the brackets with a colon between the first and last cell. the formula on screen adds every cell from A1 to A10, not just the two cells named.
Go on.

Replicating a formula means copying it into other cells, usually by dragging the fill handle down a column or across a row. This is quicker than typing each formula and makes errors less likely. By default references are relative: the spreadsheet adjusts them to fit the new position. If D2 contains the formula on screen and it is filled down, D3 contains the formula on screen and D9 contains the formula on screen Sometimes every formula must point to one fixed cell, for example a single VAT rate, discount rate or exchange rate stored at the top of the sheet.
Right. Keep going.

This needs an absolute reference, made by putting a dollar sign in front of the column letter and the row number, such as F1 with dollar signs. When the formula on screen is filled down, the G reference changes each row but F1 with dollar signs stays locked. If the dollar signs are missed, the copied formula points at the wrong cell, often a blank one, and gives wrong results without any warning. Keeping the rate in one cell also means it can be changed once and every result updates.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
Spreadsheet?
Application software that organises data in a grid of rows and columns so it can be calculated, analysed and presented. A spreadsheet file (workbook) contains one or more worksheets.
Cell range?
A block of adjacent cells referred to together, written first cell:last cell, e dot g. B5 to B12.
Label?
Text used to identify the contents of a row or column, e dot g. Name, Age.
Value?
A number entered into a spreadsheet so that calculations can be carried out, e dot g. 5, 23.
Formula?

An instruction in a cell to carry out a calculation using operators and cell references, e dot g. the formula on screen It always starts with equals and the cell shows the result, which updates when the referenced cells change.
Spreadsheet function?
A built-in formula that does a specific job, e dot g. SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, COUNT, IF and VLOOKUP.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

Spreadsheet questions appear on every Unit 1 paper, usually worth 10 to 13 marks and based on a screenshot of a sheet. You will often be asked to write a formula or function for a named cell: SUM with a correct range, AVERAGE or MAX, or a subtraction. Full marks need the equals sign, the right function name, brackets and a colon in the range, for example the formula on screen Using x instead of times or listing cells one by one when a range was asked for loses marks. Absolute referencing is tested often: say that the reference does not change when the formula is replicated, and explain why it matters in that sheet, such as one exchange rate used by every row. Formatting questions ask you to name or describe a feature you can see, such as merge and centre, currency or wrap text. Name the feature precisely and say what it does to the cells.

Let's finish with a question for the listeners. In a tuck shop sheet, which function finds the smallest value in D2 to D6? Is it A, the formula on screen; B, the formula on screen; C, the formula on screen; D, the formula on screen?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is B: the formula on screen. MIN returns the lowest value; a colon (not a comma) shows the whole range D2 to D6.
That's it for Spreadsheets 1: structure, formatting, formulae and cell referencing. Next, try the worksheet and the quiz for this lesson on the hub.
